title: Agloe, the fake town that became real
hook: A town invented to catch map copiers ended up with a real shop.
peek: In the 1930s two mapmakers put a made-up hamlet called Agloe on a road map of New York State, as a trap for copiers. Years later a general store opened at the empty crossroads and took the name from the map.
lede: In the 1930s Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers of the General Drafting Company made a road map of New York State. At a dirt-road junction in the Catskills they added a town that did not exist, called Agloe, a jumble of their initials. If Agloe ever appeared on a rival's map, they would know it had been copied.

bullets.text: Years later someone opened a shop at the junction. Seeing Agloe on the maps, the owners named it the Agloe General Store. The place that had been invented as a trap now had a real business carrying its name.

As the story is usually told, Agloe later appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting cried foul. The defence was that Agloe was now a real place, because the county recognised it. The details of the dispute are hard to confirm.

Fake places like Agloe are called paper towns or trap streets. Since copying a map of real roads is hard to prove, a harmless invention gives mapmakers a fingerprint. Dictionaries use made-up words for the same reason.
The store eventually closed and the site is empty again. Agloe became famous through John Green's 2008 novel Paper Towns, and for a while it even appeared on Google Maps.
